Problems & solutions

Why am I so sore after workouts, and should I train again?

Understand the questions to ask about soreness, recovery and when to seek help.

By Nutrition.Fitness · 15 September 2026 · 4 min read

The short answer

Delayed soreness can follow unfamiliar or harder exercise, but pain is not proof of an effective workout. Mild soreness may allow comfortable everyday movement while you avoid hard work for the affected muscles. Sharp, worsening or severe pain needs a different response. Do not let a workout streak override symptoms, and seek urgent help for concerning signs such as severe muscle pain with dark urine.

Soreness after a new workout is common, but being unable to get downstairs is not a required stage of getting fitter. The useful question is whether you are experiencing a manageable response to unfamiliar activity or symptoms that need assessment.

Cleveland Clinic describes delayed onset muscle soreness, or DOMS, as soreness that commonly develops one to three days after unfamiliar or demanding exercise and usually eases over several days. It also explains that a productive workout does not require DOMS. Pain starting suddenly during a movement should not simply be given that label.

Before today's workout, ask three questions

Where is the discomfort? When did it begin? Can you move normally? Those details are more useful than deciding whether you are the sort of person who “pushes through”. You do not need to prove anything to the calendar reminder on your phone.

This table can help organise your next step, but it cannot diagnose an injury:

What you noticeReasonable next step
Mild delayed muscle soreness; ordinary movement remains comfortableKeep activity comfortable and give the affected muscles a break from hard training.
You are changing how you move to avoid discomfortPause the planned exercise and reassess; seek advice if you are unsure.
Sharp pain, worsening pain or substantial swellingGet appropriate clinical advice rather than treating it as routine soreness.
Severe muscle symptoms with dark urine or unusual weaknessSeek urgent medical attention.

The NHS advises contacting 111 for severe or worsening injury pain, marked swelling or inability to bear weight. The CDC identifies severe muscle pain, dark urine and unusual weakness as warning signs of rhabdomyolysis, which needs immediate medical assessment. You do not need every sign before seeking help.

Can you do something else?

With ordinary mild soreness, comfortable everyday movement may be reasonable while the affected area recovers. Cleveland Clinic advises avoiding intense exercise for sore muscles. “Something else” should not be a clever way to repeat the same painful movement under a different name.

For example, replacing a demanding leg workout with an even harder circuit containing squats does not give your legs much of a break. Choosing a comfortable walk may be more sensible for some people; for others, rest is the better decision. Base the choice on symptoms and your circumstances, not on needing to fill a workout box.

If you have an injury or a rehabilitation programme, follow your clinician's advice. A general article cannot tell you exactly when your particular muscle or joint is ready.

Use the experience to improve the plan

After you are comfortable again, look at what changed before the soreness. Was it the first session after a long break? A completely new exercise? Several new things at once? Write down the change so you can discuss a more suitable starting level.

You do not have to abandon an activity because the first attempt was too much. You may need a different amount, variation or pace. A useful provider should be able to explain that adjustment and tell you when they need to refer the question elsewhere.

If almost every workout leaves you struggling with everyday tasks, that is a reason to review suitability. It should not be promoted as evidence that the membership is working particularly well.

Ask what happens when you need to rest

Before buying a programme, look beyond the exercise videos. Can sessions be moved? Does the plan include easier options? Is progress presented in a way that allows sensible rest? What happens when you report pain?

A streak can be a helpful reminder, but it should never become an instruction to ignore symptoms. You should not be made to feel that taking an appropriate rest day means starting your entire journey again.

Do you need a recovery purchase?

Do not assume you need a tub, gadget or expensive treatment because you feel sore. First resolve whether the activity was suitable and whether symptoms need medical attention. A product cannot answer those questions.

If the difficulty is choosing manageable sessions, use the programme information to compare starting levels and adaptations. If the difficulty is pain, choose appropriate professional advice. The goal is to return to a routine that serves you, not to become better at tolerating an unsuitable one.

Sources and checks

Information checked on 15 September 2026.

  • Cleveland Clinic: Delayed onset muscle soreness
  • NHS: Sprains and strains
  • CDC: Rhabdomyolysis signs and symptoms
